{{Short description|Theorem relating the diameter of a point set to the minimum radius of an enclosing ball}}
{{No footnotes|date=May 2025}}
In [[geometry]], '''Jung's theorem''' is an [[inequality (mathematics)|inequality]] between the [[diameter]] of a set of points in any [[Euclidean space]] and the [[radius]] of the [[circumradius|minimum enclosing ball]] of that set. It is named after [[Heinrich Jung]], who first studied this inequality in 1901. Algorithms also exist to solve the [[smallest-circle problem]] explicitly.

== Statement ==
Consider a [[compact set]]

:<math>K \subset \mathbb{R}^n</math>

and let

:<math>d = \max_{p,q\,\in\, K} \| p - q \|_2</math>

be the [[diameter]] of ''K'', that is, the largest [[distance|Euclidean distance]] between any two of its points. Jung's theorem states that there exists a [[closed ball]] with radius

:<math>r \leq d \sqrt{\frac{n}{2(n+1)}}</math>

that contains ''K''.  The boundary case of equality is attained by the regular ''n''-[[simplex]].

== Jung's theorem in the plane ==
The most common case of Jung's theorem is in the [[Euclidean plane|plane]], that is, when ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2. In this case the theorem states that there exists a [[circle]] enclosing all points whose radius satisfies

:<math>r \leq \frac{d}{\sqrt{3}},</math>

and this bound is as tight as possible since when ''K'' is an [[equilateral triangle]] (or its three vertices) one has <math>r = \frac{d}{\sqrt{3}}.</math>

== General metric spaces ==
For any [[Bounded_set#Definition_in_a_metric_space|bounded set]] <math>S</math> in any [[metric space]], <math>d/2\le r\le d</math>. The first inequality is implied by the [[triangle inequality]] for the center of the ball and the two diametral points, and the second inequality follows since a ball of radius <math>d</math> centered at any point of <math>S</math> will contain all of <math>S</math>. Both these inequalities are tight:

* In a ''uniform metric space'', that is, a space in which all distances are equal, <math>r=d</math>. 
* At the other end of the spectrum, in an [[injective metric space]] such as the [[taxicab geometry|Manhattan distance]] in the plane, <math>r=d/2</math>: any two closed balls of radius <math>d/2</math> centered at points of <math>S</math> have a non-[[empty set|empty]] [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]], therefore all such balls have a common intersection, and a radius <math>d/2</math> ball centered at a point of this intersection contains all of <math>S</math>. 

Versions of Jung's theorem for various [[non-Euclidean geometry|non-Euclidean geometries]] are also known (see e.g. Dekster 1995, 1997).
